findings.text: The freq_attr structure pairs a generic attribute with a read hook that formats policy state into a caller buffer and a write hook that consumes a bounded input buffer to adjust policy state. Both hooks receive the owning policy alongside their buffer arguments, keeping per-policy presentation separate from core mechanics.

Attribute helper macros generate static objects whose access mode and handler wiring follow the requested variant. Read-only forms expose only a show handler with mode 0444, read-write forms expose a show handler together with a store handler with mode 0644, write-only forms expose only a store handler with mode 0200, and one read-only form accepts a caller-supplied mode. Global variants apply the same pattern to kobject attributes, and handler names derive from the attribute name with a show prefix together with a store prefix.

The driver descriptor is the central registration record for a frequency driver. It holds a fixed-length textual name, a flag word, opaque driver-private data, a table of extra frequency attributes, a boost enable flag and grouped operation hooks. Hooks divide into policy lifecycle, frequency selection, measurement and platform integration, letting the core drive diverse hardware through one uniform record.

Lifecycle handling expects a mandatory init hook and a verify hook for each policy. Optional transitions include online and offline pairing, plus exit teardown, suspend and resume power steps, a ready announcement after full initialization, and a bios_limit query for firmware caps. Verify operates on policy data rather than live policy state, keeping limit checks separate from activation.

Frequency control offers alternative styles. A driver supplies either setpolicy for policy-driven operation or the target family for direct requests, plus fast_switch for atomic changes, get for reading a CPU clock, update_limits for firmware-driven bound changes, and scale_freq_ref for capacity reference. The core selects among these according to which hooks are populated.

Stable intermediate stepping pairs the query hook get_intermediate together with the apply hook target_intermediate before jumping to the requested index. A zero answer from the query means no intermediate step, so the core calls the indexed setter directly. The pair is valid only with the indexed setter target_index populated and without async notification advertised, and the core owns transition notifications on these paths so drivers skip them. The async rule refers to CPUFREQ_ASYNC_NOTIFICATION.

Performance-hint extension builds on the fast path. The adjust_perf hook accepts minimum, target, maximum and capacity hints for drivers with internal performance representation, and it may appear only when the fast hook fast_switch is also present because the scheduler governor falls back to the latter when scale invariance is disabled under specific conditions. Boost combines a boolean flag boost_enabled with a separate per-policy setter set_boost, while the enrollment hook register_em handles energy-model enrollment between policy setup and governor start.

Efficiency preference is carried by CPUFREQ_RELATION_E on bit two. Combining that modifier with the low base gives CPUFREQ_RELATION_LE, with the high base gives CPUFREQ_RELATION_HE, and with the close base gives CPUFREQ_RELATION_CE, each preserving direction while adding efficiency bias.

Driver capability flags occupy distinct low bits. Bit zero requests limit refresh on firmware events, bit one declares constant loops, bit two marks the driver as a cooling device, bit three advertises per-policy governor capability, bit four selects asynchronous notification, bit five demands an initial frequency check, and bit six opts out of automatic dynamic switching.

Thermal control is enabled only when the thermal configuration is active and the driver advertises cooling-device capability. Limit sanitization first clamps the policy maximum into the supplied bounds and then clamps the minimum into the lower bound and the already-clamped maximum, preserving min-not-above-max. A CPU-specific wrapper applies the same sanitization using the policy CPU info extremes.

In the routed fallback configuration several hooks are inert. Suspend and resume perform no action, notifier registration and unregistration report success without effect, the schedutil-governor test always reports false, boost query always reports disabled while software boost control reports unsupported, and the architecture frequency-scale hook accepts CPU mask plus current and maximum frequencies but takes no action.

Notification multiplexing uses small integer identifiers. Transition and policy lists are distinguished as zero and one respectively. Within transitions, pre-change and post-change phases are zero and one. Within policy events, creation and removal are likewise zero and one. Identical numeric values across different families are disambiguated by list or phase context, not by global uniqueness.

Policy and frequency changes follow two-phase announcements. Policy lifecycle emits a creation event when a policy appears and a removal event when it disappears. Each frequency transition emits a pre-change notice before the switch and a post-change notice after, allowing observers to bracket the window where the clock is unstable.

Frequency-proportional scaling multiplies an input value by a multiplier then divides by a divisor, with width-specific handling to preserve precision on 32-bit and 64-bit longs. The 32-bit path widens the intermediate product before division, while the 64-bit path computes in native width. Callers supply old value, divisor and multiplier; division by zero behavior is not defined in the fragment.

Static policy selectors use consecutive small integers. Unknown is zero, powersave is one and performance is two, giving governors and drivers a compact enumeration for fixed-policy operation distinct from dynamic governor selection.

Governor descriptor carries a fixed-length name, lifecycle hooks for initialization, teardown, start, stop and limit reaction, optional fixed-frequency show and store hooks, a list linkage for global registration, an owner module reference and a flag byte. Initialization and teardown bracket the governor lifetime while start and stop bracket active regulation on a given policy.

Governor capability flags occupy low bits. Bit zero advertises dynamic switching support and bit one requests strict target enforcement, letting the core tailor transition handling to governor guarantees.

Governor registration helpers generate module entry points that forward to core register and unregister operations. The init helper runs at core initialization time and returns the registration status, while the exit helper runs at module unload and releases the governor. Both derive their entry names from the governor identifier.

Limit enforcement compares the current frequency against policy bounds and nudges the hardware toward compliance when outside. If current exceeds maximum the driver is asked for maximum with a high-efficiency relation, and if current lies below minimum the driver is asked for minimum with a low-efficiency relation. In-bounds states require no action.

Governor attribute set groups a kobject for presentation with a list of attached policies, a mutex serializing updates and a usage counter tracking active references. The set acts as the shared control node for governors operating across multiple policies.

The governor attribute set embeds an update mutex together with its policy list and usage count. The placement identifies this mutex as the serialization point for changes to membership and reference state.

Conversion from a generic kobject pointer back to its enclosing governor attribute set uses container-relative addressing. Callers pass the kobject address and receive the owning set address, enabling callbacks to recover policy context from the object they are invoked on.

Governor tunable descriptor pairs a generic attribute with show and store hooks operating on an attribute set rather than a single policy. The show hook renders set-wide state into a buffer while the store hook consumes a bounded input buffer to adjust it, supporting tunables shared across policies.

Frequency table control markers use inverted unsigned values. The invalid-entry marker is all bits set, while the table terminator is all bits set except the lowest bit cleared. Iteration stops at the terminator and skips invalid entries, so neither marker denotes a usable frequency.

Per-entry table flags occupy low bits. Boost capability is indicated by the lowest bit and inefficiency by the next bit, allowing entries to be marked for opportunistic overdrive or for deprioritization during efficient selection.

Frequency table entry holds a flag word, an opaque driver-data slot untouched by the core, and a frequency in kilohertz. Entries need not appear in sorted order; ordering, when present, is recorded separately in the policy and determines which search variant applies.

Table traversal helpers iterate by pointer until the terminator, optionally tracking an index. Valid-only forms skip entries marked invalid, while efficiency-aware forms additionally skip inefficient entries when the caller enables efficiency filtering. Index-tracking forms start counting at zero and advance in step with the pointer, giving each visited entry a dense position.

Low-biased index search first clamps the target into the supplied minimum and maximum, then dispatches on table order. For ascending tables it returns the first allowed entry at or above target, falling back to the last seen entry when all lie below. For descending tables it prefers an exact match, otherwise tracks the most recent entry above target and returns the current entry when no higher entry exists or the tracked higher entry once the scan drops below target.

High-biased search mirrors the low-biased flow with inverted comparison. After clamping, ascending scans seek an exact match, remember the latest entry below target and resolve edge cases where no lower entry exists, while descending scans return the first allowed entry at or below target and otherwise retain the last higher entry as fallback. Both preserve efficiency filtering when requested.

Closest-match search extends the high and low scans with distance comparison. Exact matches win immediately; otherwise the scan remembers the nearest entry on one side of target and, upon crossing to the other side, compares absolute gaps to choose the nearer of the remembered and current entries. When no entry exists on the remembered side the first crossing entry is returned directly.

Unified target resolution enables efficiency filtering only when the policy advertises efficiency data and the caller sets the efficiency modifier, then strips the modifier before dispatch. Unsorted tables delegate to a separate unsorted resolver; sorted tables dispatch to low, high or close search by base relation, warning and returning zero on unknown relations. If the chosen index falls outside the requested bounds while filtering is active, the resolver retries once without filtering. Limit testing rejects negative indexes and accepts only frequencies inside the interval, and valid-entry counting walks to the terminator tallying non-invalid entries, yielding zero for a missing table.

Efficiency marking has supported and unsupported builds. The supported form rejects unsorted tables, scans valid entries for an exact frequency match, sets the inefficient flag on the match and records that efficiency data is available, returning an invalid-argument error when no match exists. The fallback build unconditionally reports invalid argument, indicating annotation is unavailable in that configuration.

Performance-domain sharing discovery resolves a CPU device node and its phandle arguments for a named list and cell, then builds a mask of CPUs sharing identical arguments. The primary CPU is always included; other possible CPUs are probed individually, skipped on resolution failure, added on argument equality and released after comparison. One configuration performs this walk while an alternate configuration reports operation unsupported without touching the mask.

CPU mask manipulation sets the bit for a given identifier after range validation. Possible-CPU iteration has two builds: a single-CPU build that visits only identifier zero, and a general build that walks the global possible mask. Sharing discovery relies on the general form to enumerate candidates, while constrained builds see only the boot CPU.

Energy-model enrollment forwards the policy CPU device and its related-CPU mask to the operating-performance-point layer. The helper resolves the device from the policy CPU identifier and passes the policy sharing mask unchanged, delegating persistence and accounting to that layer.
The CPU hotplug header defines a conventional include guard to prevent multiple inclusion. No behavioral contract is carried by this fragment beyond idempotent inclusion.

Efficiency filtering interacts sharply with table order and bounds. Requesting efficiency on an unsorted table bypasses filtering entirely via the unsorted path, marking inefficiency on unsorted tables fails outright, and an out-of-bounds efficient pick silently retries without filtering which can surprise callers expecting strict efficiency. Unknown base relations trigger a one-time warning and yield index zero, risking an unintended frequency if callers ignore the warning.
